title: Lumbar Spinal Stenosis
case: Case: A 68-year-old retired teacher has bilateral buttock and thigh heaviness after 5 minutes of walking. Sitting relieves it within a minute. She can cycle for 20 minutes without symptoms. Pulses are normal, reflexes are normal at rest, no saddle or bladder symptoms.

Working diagnosis: lumbar spinal stenosis with neurogenic claudication. Plan: education, stationary cycling, supported walking, hip and trunk strengthening, balance, monitoring; discuss specialist referral if walking does not improve.
qa: Why does leaning forward help? Flexion is thought to enlarge the space for the nerves, whereas extension may narrow it. This explanation is accepted but not fully proven for every patient.

How do you separate vascular from neurogenic claudication? Check pulses and skin, and ask what relieves symptoms. Relief by standing still suggests vascular, while relief by sitting or flexing suggests neurogenic [Ref - to verify].
Why is a scan not enough for diagnosis? Many people with a narrow canal on a scan have no symptoms, so the clinical picture matters.
When do you refer urgently? With saddle or bladder symptoms, rapidly worsening weakness or falls, or signs of acute limb ischaemia.
Why is cycling useful in this patient? The flexed position is usually better tolerated, so it allows exercise that builds fitness without provoking symptoms.

fields.Purpose: Measure how far or how long the patient walks before symptoms start, and what eases them
fields.Position: Standing, then walking on a flat path or treadmill at the patient's own pace
fields.Action: Ask the patient to walk until symptoms begin, then record time or distance. Ask them to sit and then stand and walk again; record recovery time and the posture that eases symptoms. Repeat neurological checks after walking if a deficit is suspected
fields.Positive: Symptoms reproduced by walking and relieved by sitting or flexion
fields.Limits: Not specific alone. Vascular claudication also appears with walking. Compare relief pattern
fields.Next step: Check pulses and consider vascular referral if the relief pattern does not fit

fields.Action: Ask the patient to stand in lumbar extension for a short time (some versions use about 30 seconds) [Ref - to verify]
fields.Positive: Leg symptoms start or increase and ease when flexing

redFlags.Finding: Saddle numbness, bladder or bowel change, sexual dysfunction

redFlags.Urgency: Urgent same day or next day

redFlags.Finding: Cold, painful, pale or pulseless leg

manual.name: Gentle lumbar flexion-biased mobilization
manual.finding: Stiff painful spine, relief with flexion
manual.application: Side-lying or supine knee-to-chest mobilization, gentle oscillations

manual.name: Hip and thoracic mobilization
manual.why: Reduces compensatory stress on the lumbar spine

manualNotes: Preferred starting choice: exercise and walking strategies. A combined manual therapy and exercise program has shown benefit in some trials, but evidence is limited and uncertain [Ref - to verify]. Avoid techniques that force extension. Do not claim that manual therapy widens the canal.
Is it working? Look for longer walking distance, easier standing and better confidence.

exercise.Objective: Build endurance in a flexed position
exercise.Steps: Easy resistance, upright or slightly forward

exercise.Exercise: Walking with a support (trolley, walking poles)
exercise.Starting dose: Walk to first symptoms, rest in flexion, repeat several times

exercise.Steps: Lying on back, bring knees to chest

exerciseNotes: Symptom rule: brief leg symptoms that settle with a short rest are acceptable. Persistent worsening, new weakness or any saddle or bladder symptoms means stop and reassess.

modalities.name: Traction
modalities.comment: Evidence is limited and mixed [Ref - to verify]

pathway: Leg symptoms on walking and standing, eased by sitting or flexion, with preserved pulses? Yes: working diagnosis is neurogenic claudication from lumbar stenosis.
Weak pulses or relief only by standing still? Consider vascular referral.
Stable, mild to moderate? Yes: start conservative care.

Disabling walking limit, severe or progressive weakness, or no improvement after a reasonable period of conservative care? Discuss with a spine specialist about imaging and surgical opinion [Ref - to verify].
Visit 1: screen for CES and vascular causes; explain that symptoms are often manageable and that the aim is to improve walking and confidence.
Early: teach positions of relief, begin cycling or supported walking, gentle exercise.
Middle: build leg and trunk strength and balance; add longer walking intervals.
